messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Metropolis not working with models with data
parts:
On Monday, May 20, 2013 11:06:06 AM UTC-4, Peter Li wrote:
When I run BUGS examples with any variation of metropolis (unit, diag, or dense), the sampler isn't moving anywhere new. I'm not sure what is causing this, but a few weeks ago when I had run a few of the BUGS examples with metropolis, it definitely moved at least.

You can try to git bisect the issue with a test.sh script like

#! /bin/bash
STAN_HOME=/opt/stan/ # change
cd ${STAN_HOME}
make clean-all &>/dev/null
make my_test &> /dev/null # change
exit $?

You just have to change my_test to whatever narrowly tests for the problem and returns 0 on success.

One issue that you may have is that the test you are using today might not have existed far enough back in the past. If so, you might be able to add a line that does

git cherry-pick SHA

where SHA is the commit that implements the test.

Another issue you might have is that for some commits, the test might not compile due to unrelated bugs in Stan at the time. If so, then you want to exit with return code 125 when it doesn't compile, exit with return code 0 when it succeeds in moving, and exit with any other return code when it compiles but does not move.

With all that, then you just need to do

git bisect start
git bisect good good_SHA # where good_SHA is the first commit that is known to move
git bisect run bash test.sh

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Metropolis not working with models with data
parts:
In general, you'd have to reject the entire proposal.
It's just a proposal with 0 density, so there's really
nothing special about it.

But for Stan, our variable declarations imply transforms that
make sure all of the parameters are always in bounds.

The generated model code includes the transforms you need.
You can inspect how they work with HMC.

For example, if you have the following model:

parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
}

Then what you get for the log probability function is NOT

cauchy_log(sigma,0,5)

What you get is this:

cauchy_log(exp(sigma),0,5) + sigma;

The exp() transform makes sure the argument to cauchy_log
is positive.

The extra +sigma comes in from the change of scale implied by
the change of variables. In the univariate case on the log scale,
you add the log of the absolute value of the derivative of the
transform exp() at sigma.

If you don't understand univariate changes of variables or its
generalization (which involves the determinant of the Jacobian of
the transform), check out the variable transformation section near
the end of the Stan manual. It goes over the general idea and also
the specific transforms used by Stan for various constraints.

- Bob
